connectors.description: Airtable records: read, create, update and delete a record in a base's table

auth.name: airtable.access_token
auth.subject: unstated
auth.description: Airtable access token sent as a bearer — a personal access token or an OAuth-issued one

operations.description: Read one record from a table — its cell values are under `fields` in the response, keyed by column name. Returns every column the token can see, in Airtable's default JSON cell format: narrowing or reformatting them needs the `fields[]` and `cellFormat` query parameters this connector cannot encode

outputs.name: createdTime
outputs.description: When the record was created

outputs.name: fields
outputs.description: The record's cell values, keyed by column name. Individual columns are not enumerated: they are the base's own schema, which differs per base and changes at runtime — recording the envelope is what a consumer cannot infer

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The record's id

operations.description: Create one record in a table. Cell values are supplied under `fields`, keyed by column name, and must already be in the exact JSON form each column expects — Airtable's `typecast` coercion cannot be requested yet (see the connector's notes). The created record, with its `rec…` id, is in the response

outputs.name: createdTime
outputs.description: When the record was created

outputs.name: fields
outputs.description: The created record's cell values as Airtable stored them, keyed by column name. Computed and formula columns appear here having been evaluated

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The created record's id — what later calls address it by

operations.description: Update one record's cell values. The write is sparse: only the columns named in `fields` change and every other column of the record is left exactly as it was. Values must already be in the form each column expects — `typecast` coercion cannot be requested yet. The updated record is in the response

outputs.name: createdTime
outputs.description: When the record was created — unchanged by an update

outputs.name: fields
outputs.description: The record's cell values after the update, keyed by column name. Every column is returned, not only the changed ones

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The record's id

operations.description: Delete one record and every cell value in it. There is no API route back: Airtable's trash and revision history are UI features on a retention window, not endpoints, so a flux run cannot undo this. Responds `{"id": …, "deleted": true}`

outputs.name: deleted
outputs.description: Always `true` on a 2xx. Airtable reports a record that was already gone as a 404 rather than as `false`

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The id of the record that was deleted

connectors.description: Algolia search: list an application's indices, search one, and read, save or delete a single record by its object id

auth.name: algolia.api_key
auth.subject: unstated
auth.description: An Algolia API key with the ACLs this connector needs: `search` and `browse` for the reads, `addObject` and `deleteObject` for the writes. Scope it to the indices this connection should reach rather than using the Admin key

operations.description: List the indices in this Algolia application, with each index's record count and size. This is the call that discovers the index names every other operation here takes

outputs.name: items
outputs.description: The application's indices

outputs.name: nbPages
outputs.description: How many pages of indices exist. This connector requests only the first

operations.description: Search one index and return the matching records. Algolia ranks results by its own configured relevance, so the order is the index's, not this connector's; `hits_per_page` and `page` walk the result set, and `filters` narrows it with Algolia's filter syntax over the index's own attributes

outputs.name: exhaustiveNbHits
outputs.description: False when `nbHits` is an approximation, which Algolia does for very large result sets

outputs.name: hits
outputs.description: The matching records, in Algolia's ranked order. Each hit is the stored record itself — its attributes are this index's own content and are not knowable at build time — plus `objectID` and Algolia's `_highlightResult` annotations

outputs.name: nbHits
outputs.description: How many records matched in total, which may exceed what this page returned

outputs.name: nbPages
outputs.description: How many pages the result set has at this `hitsPerPage`

outputs.name: page
outputs.description: The page that was returned, counting from 0

outputs.name: params
outputs.description: Echoes the search parameters Algolia actually applied, URL-encoded

outputs.name: processingTimeMS
outputs.description: How long Algolia spent on the query, in milliseconds

outputs.name: query
outputs.description: Echoes the search text

operations.description: Read one record from an index by its object id. Returns the stored record as it is; its attributes are this index's own content model, so nothing here can name them

outputs.name: objectID
outputs.description: The record's own id, echoed back

operations.description: Save one record at a known object id, creating it if it does not exist and REPLACING it wholesale if it does. This is not a partial update: attributes absent from the body are removed from the stored record. Algolia applies the write asynchronously, so the response's `taskID` is an acknowledgement of acceptance rather than of visibility, and a search run immediately afterwards may still return the old record

outputs.name: objectID
outputs.description: The id the record was stored under, echoed back

outputs.name: taskID
outputs.description: Algolia's own id for the asynchronous indexing task. The write is accepted when this returns and visible to search some time after; this connector declares no operation that waits on it

outputs.name: updatedAt
outputs.description: When Algolia accepted the write

operations.description: Delete one record from an index by its object id. The record is gone with no undo route in the API — restoring it means re-indexing it from the source of truth. Algolia applies the delete asynchronously, so the `taskID` acknowledges acceptance rather than visibility

outputs.name: deletedAt
outputs.description: When Algolia accepted the delete

outputs.name: taskID
outputs.description: Algolia's own id for the asynchronous delete task. The delete is accepted when this returns and visible to search some time after

connectors.description: Google Workspace: read and send Gmail messages, read and create Calendar events, read and rename Drive files

auth.name: google.access_token
auth.subject: unstated
auth.description: Google OAuth2 access token sent as a bearer; short-lived, and refreshed by the host rather than by generated Flux

operations.description: Get one Gmail message by id, in Gmail's default `full` format: headers plus the parsed MIME structure, whose body parts are base64url-encoded. Needs the `gmail.readonly` scope (or `gmail.modify`)

outputs.name: historyId
outputs.description: The mailbox history id at which this message was last changed. **A string**, despite being an integer value

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The message's id — what this operation takes

outputs.name: internalDate
outputs.description: When Gmail received it, as **epoch milliseconds in a string** — not an ISO timestamp, and not seconds. The RFC 2822 `Date` header inside `payload` may differ from it

outputs.name: labelIds
outputs.description: The labels applied, as ids: `INBOX`, `UNREAD`, `SENT`, `IMPORTANT`, `CATEGORY_PERSONAL`, plus any user label's opaque id. `UNREAD`'s presence is how read-state is expressed — there is no `read` boolean

outputs.name: payload
outputs.description: THE MESSAGE ITSELF, as a MIME tree: `{partId, mimeType, filename, headers, body, parts}`. `headers` is an **array** of `{name, value}` — so `Subject` and `From` are found by searching it, not by keying into it — and each `body.data` is **base64url-encoded**. A multipart message's text is in `parts`, not in the top-level `body`

outputs.name: sizeEstimate
outputs.description: Approximate size in bytes

outputs.name: snippet
outputs.description: A short plain-text extract of the body — the only text in this response that needs no decoding, and it is truncated

outputs.name: threadId
outputs.description: The conversation it belongs to. Several messages share one

operations.description: Send a Gmail message, supplied as a complete base64url-encoded RFC 2822 message. It is delivered immediately from the token owner's mailbox and cannot be recalled. Needs the `gmail.send` scope

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The sent message's id — the only handle on a mail that cannot be recalled, and what `google-gmail-message-get` reads back

outputs.name: labelIds
outputs.description: Typically `["SENT"]`. Google documents the response as "an instance of Message" without stating which members are populated on a send, so treat anything beyond `id` and `threadId` as possibly absent

outputs.name: threadId
outputs.description: The thread it landed in. Equal to `id` for a new conversation

operations.description: List every label in a mailbox — the system labels (`INBOX`, `SENT`, `SPAM`) and the user's own — as `{"labels": [...]}`. Needs the `gmail.readonly` scope (or `gmail.labels`)

outputs.name: labels
outputs.description: Every label in the mailbox, in one unpaginated response — there is no `nextPageToken` on this method. Only the five members below are returned by a *list*; the per-label message counts belong to a `labels.get`

operations.description: Get one calendar event: its summary, start and end, organizer, attendee list and status. Needs the `calendar.events.readonly` scope (or `calendar.readonly`)

outputs.name: attendees
outputs.description: Each `{email, displayName, organizer, self, optional, responseStatus}`, where `responseStatus` is `needsAction`, `declined`, `tentative` or `accepted` — this is how attendance is read. Absent entirely on an event with no attendees, such as every event `google-calendar-event-insert` creates. Personal data: it is a list of named people's addresses

outputs.name: conferenceData
outputs.description: The conference in full: `entryPoints` with join URLs and dial-in numbers, plus a `conferenceId`. Contains the same joinable links as `hangoutLink`

outputs.name: creator
outputs.description: Same shape; the creator need not still be the organizer

outputs.name: end
outputs.description: Same shape, and **exclusive**: an all-day event on the 30th has `end.date` of the 31st. For a recurring event this describes the first instance

outputs.name: etag
outputs.description: The resource's ETag, as a quoted string

outputs.name: hangoutLink
outputs.description: The Google Meet join link, when the event has a conference. **Anyone holding it can join the meeting**, so treat it as sensitive rather than as an ordinary URL

outputs.name: htmlLink
outputs.description: The event's page in Google Calendar — the link to give a human

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The event id — what this operation takes

outputs.name: location
outputs.description: Free text, not a structured address

outputs.name: organizer
outputs.description: `{email, displayName, self}` — who owns the event. `self` is true when it is the token's own calendar

outputs.name: recurringEventId
outputs.description: Present on an instance of a recurring event: the id of the series it belongs to

outputs.name: start
outputs.description: WHEN IT STARTS, as an object: `dateTime` (RFC 3339) for a timed event **or** `date` (`yyyy-mm-dd`) for an all-day event — never both — plus an optional IANA `timeZone`. Reading `start.dateTime` unconditionally misses every all-day event

outputs.name: status
outputs.description: **A cancelled event is still returned here**, with `cancelled`. Check this before treating the event as live

outputs.name: summary
outputs.description: The title. Absent on an event created without one, which Calendar renders as "(No title)"

operations.description: Create a timed event on a calendar. No attendees can be declared yet, so nobody is invited and no notification is sent; invite people in Calendar afterwards. Needs the `calendar.events` scope

outputs.name: attendees
outputs.description: ABSENT on every event this operation creates: no attendee can be declared yet (C-56), so nobody was invited and nobody was notified

outputs.name: creator
outputs.description: The token's own account

outputs.name: end
outputs.description: Same shape, and exclusive

outputs.name: htmlLink
outputs.description: The event's page in Google Calendar — the link to give a human

outputs.name: iCalUID
outputs.description: The RFC 5545 UID, which is what identifies this event across calendars — distinct from `id`

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The new event's id — the only handle on it, and what `google-calendar-event-get` reads back

outputs.name: organizer
outputs.description: `{email, displayName, self}` — the calendar the event was created on

outputs.name: sequence
outputs.description: The iCalendar revision number, `0` on creation

outputs.name: start
outputs.description: `{dateTime, timeZone}` as created. Calendar resolves the offset that was sent into its own representation, so this may not be the literal string that was sent

outputs.name: status
outputs.description: `confirmed` on a freshly created event

outputs.name: summary
outputs.description: Echoes the title that was sent

operations.description: Get one calendar's own metadata — its summary, description, location and time zone. This is the calendar, not its events: use `google-calendar-event-get` for one of those. Needs the `calendar.readonly` scope

outputs.name: conferenceProperties
outputs.description: `{allowedConferenceSolutionTypes}` — which conferencing this calendar permits (`hangoutsMeet`, `eventHangout`, `eventNamedHangout`)

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The calendar's address, e.g. `you@example.com` or `team@group.calendar.google.com`. Asking for `primary` resolves to this

outputs.name: location
outputs.description: Free-text geographic location of the calendar

outputs.name: summary
outputs.description: The calendar's title

outputs.name: timeZone
outputs.description: The calendar's own IANA time zone, e.g. `Europe/Berlin`. **This is what an event's offset should be computed from** — `google-calendar-event-insert` cannot send a `timeZone`, so the caller has to apply the right offset itself

operations.description: Get one Drive file's metadata — its id, name and MIME type. This never returns file content: downloading needs `alt=media`, which is a query parameter and therefore unavailable (C-30). Needs the `drive.metadata.readonly` scope (or `drive.readonly`)

Rename a Drive file: sets its name and changes nothing else. It does not move, share, trash or replace the file's content. Needs the `drive.file` scope for files this token created, or `drive` for any other

auth.name: hubspot.access_token
auth.subject: unstated
auth.description: HubSpot private-app access token (pat-…) with crm.objects.contacts.read/write, crm.objects.companies.read and crm.objects.deals.read

operations.description: Read one contact by record id. Returns only HubSpot's default contact properties — name, email and record timestamps; a custom property needs a `properties` projection this connector cannot express yet

outputs.name: archived
outputs.description: True for a record in the recycle bin

outputs.name: archivedAt
outputs.description: Present only on an archived record

outputs.name: associations
outputs.description: Related records — companies, deals, tickets — keyed by object type. Returned only when asked for. Present on this read schema and absent from the create's

outputs.name: createdAt
outputs.description: When the record was created — an ISO timestamp here, unlike the epoch-milliseconds string the equivalent `createdate` property carries

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The record id (`hs_object_id`) **as a string**, even though this operation takes it as a number

outputs.name: properties

Which keys are present depends on the portal's own property set and on the `properties` projection this connector cannot send

outputs.name: propertiesWithHistory

operations.description: Create a contact from an email address. HubSpot treats email as the contact's unique identifier and rejects a duplicate with 409. The new record is visible to everyone in the portal and can be enrolled by a workflow, which may send it marketing email

outputs.name: properties
outputs.description: The created record's properties, keyed by internal name, EVERY VALUE A STRING. HubSpot fills in more than was sent — `createdate`, `lastmodifieddate` and `hs_object_id` at minimum

outputs.name: warnings
outputs.description: Non-fatal complaints about the create — a property HubSpot ignored, for instance. Present only on the create schema, and worth reading: the call still succeeded

operations.description: Overwrite a contact's first and last name. Both are written on every call — this operation replaces them rather than merging, so re-send the one you are not changing (read it first with hubspot-contact-get). The change is visible to everyone in the portal and can trigger a workflow
Read one company by record id. Returns only HubSpot's default company properties — name, domain and record timestamps

outputs.name: associations
outputs.description: Related contacts, deals and tickets. Returned only when asked for

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The company's record id, as a string

outputs.name: properties
outputs.description: The company's property values, keyed by internal name (`name`, `domain`, `createdate`, `hs_lastmodifieddate`, `hs_object_id`). EVERY VALUE IS A STRING — including numeric properties such as `numberofemployees` and `annualrevenue`

outputs.name: propertiesWithHistory
outputs.description: Returned only when asked for, which this connector cannot do

operations.description: Read one deal by record id. Returns only HubSpot's default deal properties — name, amount, stage, pipeline and close date

outputs.name: associations
outputs.description: The contacts and companies on the deal. Returned only when asked for

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The deal's record id, as a string

outputs.name: properties
outputs.description: The deal's property values, keyed by internal name (`dealname`, `amount`, `dealstage`, `pipeline`, `closedate`, `hs_object_id`). EVERY VALUE IS A STRING — `amount` arrives as `"1500.00"` and `closedate` as an ISO string, so a numeric or date comparison has to convert first. `dealstage` and `pipeline` are per-portal internal ids, not display names

outputs.name: propertiesWithHistory
outputs.description: Returned only when asked for

auth.name: jira.api_token
auth.subject: unstated
auth.description: Atlassian API token; the user half is the account email that minted it

operations.description: Read one Jira issue by key (`PROJ-123`) or numeric id — summary, description, status, assignee, reporter and every other configured field. Returns Jira's full default field set, including custom fields, because narrowing it needs the `fields` query parameter this connector cannot encode. Text fields are wiki markup, not rich content

outputs.name: changelog
outputs.description: Change history, when expanded. Not requested by this operation

outputs.name: expand
outputs.description: Comma-separated names of the parts that *could* be expanded — a hint, not data

outputs.name: fields
outputs.description: EVERY FIELD OF THE ISSUE, one level down — `summary`, `description`, `status`, `assignee`, `reporter`, `priority`, `issuetype`, `project`, `created`, `updated`, plus every custom field as `customfield_NNNNN`. Jira's schema declares no member of this map, because the members are whatever the site has configured, so nothing is enumerated here. `status` is a nested object (`{name, statusCategory}`), not a string, and text fields are wiki markup

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The issue's numeric id, **as a string** — Jira returns ids as strings throughout

outputs.name: key
outputs.description: The issue key, e.g. `PROJ-123`. It changes if the issue moves project; the id does not

outputs.name: renderedFields
outputs.description: The same fields rendered to HTML, when asked for. Not requested by this operation

outputs.name: self
outputs.description: The issue's own API URL

operations.description: Create a Jira issue in a project. Visible to everyone with access to the project and notifies its watchers. Only project, summary and issue type are set: a description cannot be sent yet (see the connector's notes), so file the detail as a comment afterwards. Returns the new issue's id, key and self URL

outputs.name: id
outputs.description: The new issue's numeric id, as a string

outputs.name: key
outputs.description: The new issue's key, e.g. `PROJ-123`. This is what every following call addresses it by — nothing else in the response identifies it

outputs.name: transition
outputs.description: Present when the create asked for a transition: its own `{status, errorCollection, warningCollection}`. A failure here does not fail the create, so a `201` can still mean the transition did not happen

outputs.name: watchers
outputs.description: Same shape, for watchers the create asked to add

operations.description: Read the comments on a Jira issue, oldest first. Returns Jira's first default-sized page only: paging needs the `startAt` and `maxResults` query parameters this connector cannot encode, so an issue with a long discussion is truncated. Comment bodies are wiki markup

outputs.name: comments
outputs.description: The comments, oldest first. Bodies are Jira wiki markup

outputs.name: maxResults
outputs.description: How many comments the page could hold, chosen by Jira

outputs.name: startAt
outputs.description: The offset this page starts at — 0 here, since this operation cannot send one

outputs.name: total
outputs.description: How many comments the issue has in total. **Greater than the length of `comments` means the discussion is truncated**, and this operation cannot fetch the rest

operations.description: Add a comment to a Jira issue. The comment is visible to everyone who can see the issue — including customers on a service-management portal — and notifies its watchers; restricting it to a project role or group is not supported yet. The body is Jira wiki markup (`*bold*`, `{code}`), not Markdown and not rich content

connectors.description: Klaviyo marketing platform: read the account a key belongs to, read and create customer profiles, read lists, and post an event that can trigger a flow. Every request carries a dated API revision the vendor requires

auth.subject: unstated
auth.description: Klaviyo private API key for one account. Travels as the whole Authorization header behind Klaviyo's own scheme word. Keys are scoped per key: one minted without the scopes the shipped operations need will authenticate, pass verification, and fail on exactly the call that needs the missing scope

operations.description: Read the Klaviyo account this API key belongs to, with its timezone, currency, industry and contact details. Returns exactly one account — a private key is scoped to one — so this is the call that answers 'which account am I connected to'. Also this connector's verify: it takes no argument and needs only the accounts:read scope

outputs.name: data
outputs.description: Always exactly one account: a private API key belongs to one account and cannot see another

outputs.name: links
outputs.description: JSON:API document links. `next` is absent here; an account list is never paginated

operations.description: List customer profiles in the account, newest first. Returns the FIRST PAGE ONLY — Klaviyo pages with an opaque `page[cursor]` query parameter this connector cannot send, so there is no way to reach later pages and no way to filter. Every profile carries personal data: an email address, often a phone number and a postal location

outputs.name: data
outputs.description: One entry per profile, first page only

outputs.name: links
outputs.description: `self`, and `next`/`prev` when more pages exist. **`next` is unusable here** — following it needs the `page[cursor]` query parameter (C-30)

operations.description: Read one customer profile by its Klaviyo id, with its identifiers, custom properties, consent state and location. Returns personal data about a named individual

Create a customer profile. At least one identifier is required — email, phone number or external id — and Klaviyo answers 409 Conflict if a profile with that identifier already exists, so this creates and never updates. The created profile can be marketed to only once it is subscribed, which this connector does not do

List the account's lists — static, opt-in collections of profiles, as opposed to segments, which are live queries and are not shipped here. Returns the FIRST PAGE ONLY; Klaviyo's `page[cursor]` query parameter cannot be sent by this connector. Returns the lists themselves, not their members

outputs.name: data
outputs.description: One entry per list, first page only

outputs.name: links
outputs.description: `self`, plus `next`/`prev` when more pages exist. `next` is unusable here (C-30)

operations.description: Post an event about a customer — a purchase, a page view, anything the account measures. THIS CAN CAUSE A MESSAGE TO BE SENT: an event triggers any Klaviyo flow built on its metric, so an email or SMS may reach the named profile immediately. Klaviyo creates the metric and the profile on first use if they do not exist. Answers 202 Accepted with no body: the event is queued, not confirmed. Pass unique_id to make a retry safe — Klaviyo records only the first event with a given unique_id for the same profile and metric

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Present only when `ok` is false: Slack's machine-readable failure code, such as `channel_not_found`, `not_in_channel` or `msg_too_long`

outputs.name: message
outputs.description: The message as Slack stored it: `text`, `type`, `subtype`, `ts`, `bot_id`, `username`, and `attachments` when there are any

outputs.name: ok
outputs.description: False on failure, with HTTP still 200. Branch on this before reading anything else — it is the only member present in both outcomes

outputs.name: ts
outputs.description: The posted message's timestamp id, e.g. `1503435956.000247`. This is what addresses the message afterwards — `slack-reactions-add`'s `timestamp`, and `thread_ts` to reply under it

operations.description: Read recent messages from a Slack channel, newest first. Slack answers HTTP 200 even on failure: check `ok` in the response body, where an error such as `channel_not_found` appears at `error`

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Present only when `ok` is false: `channel_not_found`, `not_in_channel` or `invalid_arguments`

outputs.name: has_more
outputs.description: True when the channel holds older messages than this page returned. This connector cannot page — see the header comment on the missing cursor — so a true here means the caller is seeing a window, not the history

outputs.name: messages
outputs.description: The messages, newest first. Each carries at least `type`, `ts` and `text`; a user message also carries `user`, and a bot or system message carries a `subtype` instead

outputs.name: ok
outputs.description: False on failure, with HTTP still 200. Branch on this first

outputs.name: response_metadata
outputs.description: Carries `next_cursor`, the cursor for the following page. It cannot be sent back by this connector (C-30)

operations.description: Look up one Slack user by id — display name, real name, time zone and whether they are a bot. Slack answers HTTP 200 even on failure: check `ok` in the response body, where an error such as `user_not_found` appears at `error`

outputs.name: error
outputs.description: Present only when `ok` is false: typically `user_not_found`

outputs.name: ok
outputs.description: False on failure, with HTTP still 200. Branch on this first

outputs.name: user

outputs.description: Present only when `ok` is false, with HTTP still 200: `already_reacted`, `message_not_found`, `invalid_name`, `channel_not_found` or `thread_locked`

connectors.description: Supabase project data and configuration: describe the tables the API exposes, read a table's rows, and read which sign-in methods the project has enabled. outputs.description: The project's API host, as PostgREST sees it

outputs.name: info

outputs.name: swagger
outputs.description: The OpenAPI version of this document — `2.0`

operations.description: Read rows from one table or view in this project. Returns a JSON array of row objects with every column the anon role may read; the columns are the project's own, so call supabase-schema-describe first to learn them. Row-level security decides which rows come back — an empty array means the policies matched nothing, not that the table is empty. This connector cannot filter, project or sort: pass `limit` to bound the read and do the rest in the flow

Read which sign-in methods this project has enabled, and whether self-service sign-up is open. Takes no argument and returns configuration only — no user data and no identities. Use it to decide whether a flow can offer a given provider before it tries

outputs.name: external
outputs.description: One boolean per external identity provider the project may enable — `google`, `github`, `apple`, `azure` and the rest — true where it is configured and turned on.
